title: America has always been drawn to an unelected elite. Meet the courtier class | Nancy Isenberg
text:
Americans remain awed by the extravagance of the super-rich, oddly enticed and generally accepting of the fact that the moneyed elite have privileges that they use to their own advantage.
After the Hollywood celebrity and the professional athlete, the figure who invites the most curiosity is what is colloquially termed “powerbroker”. We’re talking about the dealmaker, the inside player – or in the words of Sade’s song, a “smooth operator”.
As an unelected class, this shadow group appears to exert undue control over decisions made and directions taken by those who technically wield power. One might imagine that the recent exposure of the “Epstein class” marks a new phenomenon, a perverse dynamic operating within circles in Washington and the upper echelons of the corporate world.
In fact, there is nothing at all new here. The same type held sway at America’s founding and throughout the Gilded Age. Indeed, their history reaches as far back as court politics in old-world aristocracies.
Who is this transhistorical figure? He (and every so often she) is the courtier.
The educated elite of America’s Revolutionary generation were schooled in Baldassare Castiglione’s The Book of the Courtier (1528), which in turn informed popular guidebooks on manners, politeness and self-fashioning. George Washington admired Castiglione’s ideal of the “graceful warrior” and saw him personified in the “thorough paced courtier”, Lord William Howe, the blue-blooded commander of the British army in North America.
Titled diplomats belonged to this unofficial club as well. As Washington’s aide-de-camp, Alexander Hamilton described the French minister Chevalier de La Luzerne as one who “makes the point of being pleased with everything he sees”. The Frenchman’s “dexterity” wooed his allies; his maneuvering appeared effortless.
The courtier’s image was doubled-edged. Admired for his polished manners, he might also be reviled for exuding style over substance. To the critical eye of John Adams, who observed plenty of courtiers as a senior diplomat abroad, they were little more than sycophants, fawning on “great men in order to obtain their smiles, Esteem and Patronage and consequently their favours and Preferments”.
Yet the courtier quickly became a regular fixture at the courtly levees of presidents Washington and Adams. The celebrated Dolley Madison was far from the only first lady who accommodated herself to (and herself played) the patronage game.
Hamilton, after his appointment as secretary of the treasury, was quickly dubbed the “American Walpole”. Robert Walpole, leader of the king’s cabinet during the reigns of George I and George II, lived on in memory as one who dominated politics.
As first lord of the treasury and chancellor of the exchequer, Walpole used flattery, bribes and lavishly bestowed patronage, doing everything possible to win over both fellow Whig politicians and his Tory adversaries. Most of all, he had to impress and appease the royal family. Whether one spoke of royal authority or the president of a republic, a man could become the power behind the throne as a courtier.
Hamilton, who recognized Washington as his “aegis”, or steppingstone, on his way to the top, appreciated Walpole’s famous motto: “Every man has his price.” An ally wrote to him in 1791, citing this cunning precept. In any age, the “few great men” were those who “knew human nature” and how to “influence & operate upon temper & character”. History has fallen for mythology by failing to portray Hamilton as he truly was: the quintessential courtier.
The courtier was more than a sycophant. He effectively turned politics into a game and excelled at the art of persuasion. He plied his trade at informal social gatherings, mixing friendship with politics. Hamilton’s closest ally was William Duer, born in England, educated at Eton, and a member of the “Aristocratic Faction” headed by Hamilton’s father-in-law, Philip Schuyler.
Selected by Hamilton to serve as assistant treasury secretary, Duer made his mark as a speculator. He orchestrated lavish entertainments, kept liveried servants, and treated prospective investors to expensive wines, drawing them in to his elaborate schemes. The charming courtier lived the dazzling “life of a nobleman”, as one fellow speculator gushed, until he lost his ruffled shirt and ended his run in debtor’s prison.
A direct line links the courtier to the lobbyist, who gained a permanent foothold in political life in the era of Jacksonian democracy.
Martin Van Buren, Jackson’s cabinet-adviser-turned-successor, was known as a “fawning courtier”. He rose to power in New York, where his Albany Regency – its aristocratic name no accident – mastered the game by dispensing the “spoils” of government largesse to party insiders. The lobbyist came in various guises: he might be a well-heeled aristocrat, a respected politician and attorney, an ambitious journalist, or just a clever raconteur who, like Duer, knew how to charm.
By 1857, one journalist lamented, lobbyists ruled the US Capitol in service of a new monarch: the “almighty dollar”.
During the Gilded Age, buying influence became even more brazen. The railroad robber baron Collis Huntington showed up in Washington with trunks of cash for bribing officials. Along with the corrupt dealmaking, the courtier’s art continued to flourish.
The celebrated gourmand Samuel Cutler Ward gathered businesspeople and politicians at his elegant dinners, where wine and witty conversation forged “lobby friends”. Ward was a bona fide American aristocrat, educated at Columbia University, after which he lived in Europe; his first wife was an Astor. His cousin Ward McAllister was the impresario who orchestrated the fabled “400”, providing the invitation list for the creme-de-la-creme of New York high society.
“Every close student of Washington knows half the essential business of government is still transacted in the evening,” outside the halls of Congress, the historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr dryly remarked in 1980. The irrepressible critic Christopher Hitchens saw Schlesinger himself as a “compulsive socialite” and “courtier”, who rose to prominence in John F Kennedy’s “Camelot”.
Lewis Lapham, editor of Harper’s, wrote an entire book on the pervasiveness of the “courtier spirit” from Reagan’s administration to Clinton’s. Bill Clinton, whose seductive style borrowed from the courtier spirit, caused a media uproar when he invited friends and donors to stay overnight in the Lincoln Bedroom. Was it the “Fat Cat hotel”, as some charged, or a reward granted to the king’s favorites?
The same spirit continued to thrive at the start of a new millennium. During the contested 2000 election, George W Bush’s campaign manager, Karl Rove, earned the title of “kingmaker”, as both party conventions created their own titled peerage.
The most generous donors were accorded honorary ranks: the “Chairman’s Circle” ($500,000) for Democrats, “Regents” ($250,000), for Republicans. Not inconsequentially, the United States now stands virtually alone among western nations in awarding ambassadorships in exchange for cash-infused fealty.
The role of courtier has never just been political. As a profession, public relations is devoted to curating elite reputations. Old Hollywood gave its stars a classy makeover, and business schools in the 1950s trained future executives to exhibit an “appearance” of independence alongside the “grace” of command.
Since the 1990s, business self-help books have echoed Castiglione’s classic description of the courtier, instructing social climbers in developing a refined body language, subtly drawing attention to themselves, and always aiming to impress those above them.
Dressing for success is the direct descendant of aristocratic courtliness. After reading an account of the Russian tsar’s admission that the masses idolized him owing not to any grace, but simply his royal regalia, Mark Twain wryly observed: “Clothes do not merely make the man, the clothes are the man.” He meant it. “There is no power without clothes.”
The point is that aristocracy has infiltrated vital areas of American culture. No one gains access to the corporate boardroom or the White House without elite connections. No one climbs the ladder without impressing a superior, and self-presentation tends to carry more weight than measurable talent. The courtier’s pose is about cultivating trust, projecting a desirable image, and pleasing others. Of course, the cost of flattery is that principles are easily sacrificed.
The sordid depths to which the courtier will stoop seized headlines in the mortifying afterlife of Jeffrey Epstein. He performed a masquerade as a well-bred, college-educated elite who had moved up the ranks of the superrich. His entire life was about courting powerful men, luring them to parties and to his private island.
He understood how much belonging matters, and that, in the complicated social dance he learned to exploit, wealth and patronage is easily confused with greatness. A gilded surface conceals the rot within.
The always prescient John Adams conceded long ago that genuine merit and character would always be at a disadvantage wherever public honors were bestowed on the “lovers of gain”. Now, perhaps, it makes better sense why it took so long for his double life to be unmasked. Epstein is gone, but the courtier class waltzes on.
- This essay is adapted from Aristocracy, American Style: Class Privilege and the Persistence of Elite Power by Nancy Isenberg, to be published on 10 November by Viking, an imprint of Penguin Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House, LLC
- Nancy Isenberg recently retired as the T Harry Williams professor at Louisiana State University. She is the author of the New York Times bestseller White Trash: The 400-Year Untold History of Class in America, and two award-winning books, Fallen Founder: The Life of Aaron Burr and Sex and Citizenship in Antebellum America
